justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias with gradual upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the last observed price level, incorporating typical mean-reversion tendencies and overnight drift patterns that tend to keep prices relatively stable over such short windows. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with modest equity market momentum or fundamental tailwinds present at the time of the forecast. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, assuming continued but gradual appreciation without any major catalytic events disrupting the trend. In all three cases, the point estimates represent my best guess under a baseline scenario where prevailing conditions persist without dramatic shocks.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because most of the price-influencing information for the near term is already embedded in current market prices, and intraday or overnight volatility tends to be bounded. By one week, macroeconomic data releases, earnings surprises, Federal Reserve communications, and geopolitical developments all become meaningful contributors to variance, pushing the interval noticeably wider. At one month, these same forces operate over a longer window and can interact with each other in nonlinear ways, which is why the interval nearly doubles in width compared to the one-week horizon.

There are several specific risks that could push realized outcomes well outside my stated intervals in either direction. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in economic data — such as a sharp rise in unemployment claims, a hawkish policy surprise from a central bank, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict — could drive prices meaningfully below the lower bounds. Credit market stress or a liquidity event could amplify such moves. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish pivot in monetary policy, or a resolution of a key geopolitical risk could propel prices above my upper bounds. These tail risks are by definition underweighted in a 90% confidence interval, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes should fall outside my stated range even under well-calibrated conditions. Model misspecification, regime changes, or correlated shocks across asset classes represent additional sources of uncertainty that my intervals may not fully capture.
